essay.full:
# The bottleneck was never the motor.

A general-purpose technology is two things at once: a machine that improves quickly, and a set of buildings, habits, rules and balance sheets that change slowly around it. The headlines follow the first. The economics follow the second. This essay sets out why, what that means for AI, and which numbers the site watches to find out whether it is true.

### Folio I · the name

## Watch the variables that move slowly

Ecologists who study why ecosystems suddenly flip into a different state draw a line between two kinds of variable. Brian Walker, Stephen Carpenter and their colleagues, who work on the resilience of rangelands and lakes, call the ones people watch fast variables: the size of this year's harvest, say. Underneath sit slow variables, like the amount of organic matter in the soil, which barely move from one year to the next but decide what a dry summer does to the harvest. A fast variable swings with every shock. A slow one decides whether the shock is absorbed or tips the whole system into a different state.

AI has an abundance of fast variables. Benchmark scores, model launches and the length of task a model can finish all move monthly and all make the news. The slow variables are the ones that decide what those headlines amount to: how many firms use the technology, how much work is rebuilt around it, whether output per hour moves, which part of the industry keeps the profit, and how much of the value ends up with the people using it rather than the people selling it. This site is named after them, and it tracks five.

### Folio II · the pace

## Four machines, four clocks

American factories could buy electric power from the early 1880s. It did not show up in manufacturing productivity until the 1920s. Paul David, an economic historian at Stanford, went looking for the reason in 1990, when computers were in every office and still absent from the productivity figures, and found it in the floor plan.

A steam-era factory ran off one engine. A shaft ran the length of the building, belts dropped from it to every machine, and buildings went up several storeys to keep the shafts short. The first electric factories mostly kept this arrangement, with a motor turning the shaft where the engine had been. The large gain came later, from a small motor on each machine. With no shaft to feed, a factory could be a single storey, lighter to build, and laid out around the flow of materials instead of the flow of power. But that was a different building, and David found that the change waited on the old buildings wearing out and on an investment boom in the 1920s to pay for new ones. The motor was ready decades before the factory was.

Everett Rogers came at the same problem from a farm. He grew up in Carroll, Iowa, where his father refused to plant hybrid seed corn for years, though it plainly out-yielded the old seed, until a drought in the 1930s made the difference impossible to miss. Rogers became a rural sociologist, built on a study of how that corn spread through two Iowa towns, and spent his career on why good ideas travel slowly. His answer was that speed depends on how an innovation looks to the person deciding: whether its advantage is obvious, whether it fits the way they already work, how hard it is to learn, whether it can be tried on a small patch first, and whether they can see it working for someone else.

Put the two together and the shape of the question changes. Asking how fast AI is spreading is like asking how fast electricity spread: the answer depends on which link of the chain you time. So this site splits the chain into its links, the methods, the products built from them, the firms that try the products, and the work that finally gets rearranged, and runs a separate clock on each. METR, an independent research group that tests what AI models can do, measures the length of software task the best model can finish half the time, counted in how long the task takes a skilled person. That length has been doubling every [fact:horizon_doubling_days]. The share of American firms using AI stands at [fact:firms_using_ai], and the share of all work hours done with it at [fact:hours_assisted]. Those are not contradictory readings. They are clocks on different machines, and the gap between them is the time it takes to rebuild the factory.

[plate:clocks]

### Folio III · the money

## The money arrives first, and it is supposed to overshoot

Carlota Perez, a Venezuelan economist who studies how technologies get paid for, went through five technological revolutions: the cotton mills that began in Britain in 1771, steam and railways, steel and electricity, oil and the car, and the computer, which she dates to the microprocessor in 1971. Each unfolded in two halves. In the first, installation, financial capital leads: money that cares about the return rather than about what it builds pours into the new technology, and that indifference is exactly what lets it fund infrastructure whose worth nobody can yet calculate. Canals, railways and fibre-optic cable were all overbuilt this way. The installation half usually ends in a crash, and then comes deployment: the technology becomes ordinary, the institutions catch up, production rather than finance sets the pace, and the gains spread out of the new industry and into everyone else's.

That makes "are we in a bubble" the wrong question and "which half are we in" the right one, and the second has evidence. The clearest is how far spending on the infrastructure runs ahead of the revenue it is meant to earn. Over the past year Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Oracle spent [fact:capex_to_revenue] as much on buildings and equipment as the AI revenue we can measure, which is the leading labs' sales plus one survey of what American businesses spend on generative AI, by the venture firm Menlo Ventures. Not all of that spending is for AI, and not all AI revenue is counted, so the ratio is rough; the direction is not. The second piece of evidence is who is paying whom. [fact:vendor_financing_4q] of commitments were signed over the same four quarters in deals where the seller also funds the buyer: cloud contracts with companies that own a stake in the lab buying the computing, and chip deals in which the chip maker lends to, guarantees or invests in its customer. Demand that the seller is helping to fund is real demand, but it is also demand that stops when the funding does.

The site places itself on Perez's curve by a published rule rather than by feel. Spending at least a dollar on buildings and equipment for each dollar of AI revenue, while such deals are still being signed, is installation. Spending under half a dollar per dollar while fewer such deals are signed is deployment. Anything else is a turning point, and a change counts only when two quarters in a row agree. By that rule this is installation, which is a statement about where we are, not a forecast of how it ends.

[plate:perez]

### Folio IV · the spoils

## Inventing it and keeping the money are different problems

David Teece, a business economist at Berkeley, asked in 1986 why the firm that brings an invention to market so often watches customers and imitators do better out of it. His answer had little to do with the invention itself and a great deal to do with two things around it. The first is how easily it can be copied. The second is who owns what the invention needs in order to reach a customer, which he called complementary assets: the manufacturing, the distribution, the service network, the relationships. When copying is easy and those assets are scarce, the profit walks past the inventor and settles with whoever holds them. Being first is an event. Owning the part nobody can route around is a position.

William Nordhaus, a Yale economist later given the Nobel memorial prize in economics for bringing climate change into the study of long-run growth, asked the next question: of all the value an innovation creates, how much do the innovators keep? For the American economy from 1948 to 2001 his estimate was about two cents in the dollar. The rest went to buyers, as lower prices and better products, because profits from being ahead are competed away as others catch up.

Taken together, they say that a spectacular frontier is entirely compatible with thin and short-lived profits, and that the thing worth tracking is not how clever the models are but which part of the industry holds its margin, and for how long. The site measures that with gross profit, what is left of revenue after paying to deliver the product. It can measure three pieces: the two big chip makers, NVIDIA and AMD, from their filings; Microsoft's cloud business, the one cloud division that reports its costs; and an estimate for OpenAI and Anthropic. A year ago the chip makers took [fact:chips_gp_share_year_ago] of that gross profit. They now take [fact:chips_gp_share_now]. On the other side of the ledger, Americans, added up, say they would need to be paid [fact:consumer_surplus] a year to give up AI chatbots: value users keep rather than value anyone sells. Teece would recognise the first number, and Nordhaus the second.

[plate:stack]

### Folio V · the readings

## Where the slow variables stand

Five numbers carry the argument, and each is graded by a rule the site publishes and can change only in public, with a written reason. Firms using AI: [fact:firms_using_ai]. Work hours done with AI: [fact:hours_assisted]. Output per hour, against a year before: [fact:productivity_yoy]. The chip makers' share of the gross profit we can measure: [fact:chips_gp_share_now]. And the value users keep: [fact:consumer_surplus]. Each links to its sources, its history and the rule that grades it. Read together, they describe a technology that nothing yet shows spreading faster than an ordinary one, being paid for well ahead of its revenue, and so far rewarding the companies that sell the scarcest input.

### Folio VI · the exits

## Write down what would prove you wrong, first

An argument like this one is easy to keep forever, because every slow reading can be called early. The only defence is to name in advance what would change the conclusion and to check it on a schedule. The site's conclusions each come with that list, re-tested every night against the same data, and the list follows this essay.

One of them has already failed. The expectation that profit would drift up from the chip makers toward the model labs, as models became interchangeable, is contradicted by its own series: the labs' share grew, but the chip makers' share grew too, and the labs' gain came out of the cloud business instead. The Who profits page says so in its headline, where anyone can check it against the data. That is what a tracker is for.
essay.home:
# The bottleneck was never the motor.

American factories could buy electric power from the early 1880s, and it did not show up in the productivity statistics until the 1920s. The motors worked. What took four decades was rebuilding the factories around them, and nobody tears down a factory that is still standing. This site tracks AI on the same bet: the technology is fast, and the things it has to change are slow.

### Folio I · the pace

## Four machines, four clocks

A steam-era factory ran off one engine. A shaft ran the length of the building, belts dropped from it to every machine, and the floor plan was drawn around the shaft. Early electrification mostly swapped the engine for a big motor and left the shaft where it was. The real gain came from a small motor on every machine, which let a factory be one storey, laid out around the flow of work instead of the flow of power. That needed a new building, and firms replace buildings when the old ones wear out.

Paul David, an economic historian at Stanford, told this story in 1990 to explain why computers were not showing up in productivity either. The lag, he argued, was not a sign the technology was weak; it was the time the old plant took to wear out and be replaced. Everett Rogers, a sociologist who grew up on an Iowa farm where his father held out for years against a visibly better seed corn, found the general rule: things spread as fast as the people who must adopt them can see the advantage, try it on a small scale, and fit it into the way they already work.

So this site splits the chain into links (the methods, the products, the firms that try them, the work that gets rearranged) and times each on its own clock. METR, an independent research group that tests AI models, measures the length of software task the best model can finish half the time, counted in how long it takes a skilled person. That length has been doubling every [fact:horizon_doubling_days]. The share of firms using AI and of work hours done with it move on a different clock entirely. They are not in conflict. They are measuring different machines.

[plate:clocks]

### Folio II · the money

## The money arrives first, and it is supposed to overshoot

Carlota Perez, a Venezuelan economist who studies how technologies get financed, went through five technological revolutions, from the first cotton mills in 1771 to the microprocessor in 1971, and found the same two halves in each. First comes installation: money chasing returns pours into the new technology and pays for infrastructure long before anyone can use it all. Then a turning point, usually a crash, and then deployment, when the technology turns ordinary and its gains spread into everyone else's accounts.

Which half we are in is a question with evidence. Over the past year Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Oracle spent [fact:capex_to_revenue] as much on buildings and equipment as the AI revenue we can measure: the leading labs' sales plus one survey of what American businesses spend on generative AI. And [fact:vendor_financing_4q] of commitments were signed over the same four quarters in deals where the seller also funds the buyer, such as a cloud contract with a company that owns a stake in the lab, or a chip maker lending to its customer.

None of that says bubble. It says installation, which is a statement about where we are, not about how it ends.

[plate:perez]

## Inventing it and keeping the money are different problems

David Teece, a business economist at Berkeley, asked in 1986 why the firm that brings an invention to market so often watches its customers and imitators do better out of it. His answer had little to do with the invention. When it is easy to copy, the money goes to whoever owns what it needs to reach a customer: the manufacturing, the distribution, the relationships. For the American economy from 1948 to 2001 his answer was about two cents in the dollar; the rest went to buyers, as lower prices and better products. If AI follows that pattern, a dazzling frontier is compatible with thin, short-lived profits, and the thing to watch is who holds their margin. Measured by gross profit, what is left after paying to deliver the product, the two big chip makers, NVIDIA and AMD, took [fact:chips_gp_share_year_ago] of the gross profit we can measure a year ago, against Microsoft's cloud business and the leading labs. They take [fact:chips_gp_share_now] now.

## Write down what would prove you wrong, first

Every reading here is graded by a rule the site publishes and can change only in public, with a written reason, so a number cannot quietly be graded kindly after the fact. essay.migration:
# The bottleneck doesn't sit still. It migrates.

Making an AI model takes electricity, buildings, chips, memory, data, skilled people and money, all at the same time. Whichever of them is hardest to get sets the pace for the rest and collects most of the profit, until the industry builds its way out of the shortage. Then the shortage turns up somewhere else. This essay sets out why that happens, where the shortage has sat so far, and how this site tries to tell where it sits now.

### Folio I · the rule

## When every part is needed, the scarcest one gets paid

A factory line runs at the speed of its slowest station. Eliyahu Goldratt, an Israeli physicist who became a management writer, built a theory on that observation in The Goal, a novel about a failing factory that he wrote with Jeff Cox in 1984. A system, he argued, does only as well as its constraint allows, the constraint being whatever most limits it. Speeding up anything else is wasted effort. His method also ends on a warning: relieve the constraint and another one will limit the system instead, so go back to the first step and look again. This essay calls that constraint the bottleneck: the one input that is hardest to get, which sets the pace for everything else.

Who gets paid is an older question. David Ricardo, an English economist, asked in 1817 why landlords grew rich when bread grew dear. It can look as if high rents make corn expensive. Ricardo argued that it ran the other way: "Corn is not high because a rent is paid, but a rent is paid because corn is high." Good land is limited, so when people want more corn the extra money ends up with whoever owns the good land, and the owner need do nothing to earn it. Economists still use the word rent for income that comes from owning something scarce, as opposed to income from effort. Ricardo was writing about farms. Read a little more widely, his point is that the payment goes to whatever cannot quickly be made more of.

Put the two together and you have a rule for an industry in which every part is needed at once. The bottleneck sets the pace, and the owner of the bottleneck collects the rent. The first essay on this site met the same idea from the other side, through David Teece, a business economist who studied why inventors so often watch someone else profit from their inventions: the money settles with whoever owns what the invention cannot do without. In AI the clearest case is NVIDIA, the largest designer of AI chips, which keeps [fact:nvda_margin] of its sales as gross profit, meaning what is left after the cost of making the chips. That is what a bottleneck looks like in a company's accounts.

A margin like that is also an invitation. Every buyer who pays it has a reason to find a way around it, every rival has a reason to build a substitute, and every supplier has a reason to expand. So the rent is temporary by construction. The interesting question is never only who holds the bottleneck today. It is where the shortage goes once this one is relieved.

### Folio II · the record

## It has already moved more than once, and never in single file

It started with people. In 2012 a neural network, a program loosely modelled on connected brain cells that learns from examples, won a well-known image-recognition contest far ahead of the runner-up. It was built at the University of Toronto by Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever and their adviser Geoffrey Hinton, and it turned research in computer vision toward neural networks. What ran short was people who could build them. In 2013 Google bought Hinton's company, taking on Hinton and several of his students, and in 2014 it bought the AI company DeepMind, a deal that MIT Technology Review described as a purchase of people, not products. Yoshua Bengio, an AI researcher at the University of Montreal, estimated that year that only about fifty such experts existed in the world, many of them still graduate students.

Then computing power. In January 2020 researchers at OpenAI, one of the labs, as the companies that train the largest AI models are called, posted a paper called "Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models". It found that a language model, a program trained on text to predict what comes next, improves smoothly and predictably as its size, its training text and the computing power spent on it are scaled up together. A result like that is a reason to keep buying computing power. By 2023 buyers wanted more of it than could be made. NVIDIA's sales to data centres more than tripled in the financial year that ended in January 2024. Notice where the shortage went next. TSMC, the Taiwanese firm that manufactures those chips, said in 2023 that making the chips themselves was no problem; what was very tight was its capacity for advanced packaging, the step that joins a processor to its memory. In May 2024 SK Hynix, the leading maker of the fast stacked memory that AI chips use, said its supply was sold out for that year and almost sold out for the next.

Text looked like running short at about the same time. In 2022 researchers at DeepMind found that large language models were "significantly undertrained", meaning they had been given too little text for their size. The same year researchers at Epoch AI, a research nonprofit that publishes estimates of the data, chips, computing power and buildings behind AI, estimated that the stock of high-quality language data would be exhausted "likely before 2026". In 2024 the same group revised that: it might not happen until 2028. The labs did not wait to find out. When scraped text stops being enough, labs pay people to write better text. A 2022 paper from OpenAI trained a model on demonstrations and rankings from about forty hired contractors, and the people hired to judge the results preferred the answers of a small model trained that way to those of a model more than a hundred times its size. By the middle of 2023 Scale AI, a firm that sells such work, was advertising for trainers with expertise in law, finance and programming. In 2025 Meta took a minority stake in Scale AI, which Meta's audited accounts carry at [fact:meta_scale_price]. Surge AI, a rival, was reported in 2025 to have passed [fact:surge_revenue] in yearly revenue without having raised any outside money.

Using the models was expensive for a while, and then the price fell fast. Epoch AI reported in March 2025 that the price of reaching a fixed level of performance had been falling by between nine and nine hundred times a year, depending on the task. That is the price a provider charges, not what the model costs the provider to run, and Epoch warned that the fastest falls might not last. OpenRouter, a marketplace that gives developers one way in to hundreds of models and can route each request among them, says it started in early 2023; in August 2026 the payments company Stripe agreed to buy it. A router earns its keep while models differ widely in price and quality. The better it works, the more easily buyers move to the cheapest model that is good enough, the harder sellers must compete on price, and the less anyone needs a router.

Electricity is told last here because it may stay longest, not because it arrived last. In July 2022 Dominion Energy, a utility in Virginia, began telling data-centre companies that power for some new sites in Loudoun County would be delayed for years. In 2024 the United States Department of Energy told Congress that waits of three years were commonly quoted for a large power transformer, the substation equipment that steps voltage up for long-distance lines and down again for the sites that use the power, where under a year had been normal before the pandemic. In April 2025 the International Energy Agency projected that the electricity used by data centres would more than double by 2030.

None of this happened in single file. Computing power and data were short at the same time, and power arrived while both still were. The chart shows the overlaps. Its spans are this site's reading of the events above, not a measurement, and each one has its reason and its source in the table beneath it.

[plate:strip]

### Folio III · the tell

## Watch what the labs buy

A new bottleneck tends to satisfy three conditions at once. It limits the labs' next step, not their last one; yesterday's constraint is today's commodity. It has not yet become an industry, so there is no standard product, no quoted price and no public data, which is exactly why it is hard to see from outside. And it shows up first in what the labs buy, because a lab knows what it is short of long before anyone publishes a number about it.

That last condition can be watched. This site keeps two tallies by hand from public announcements. The first counts disclosed purchases by labs from the firms that sell training inputs, scored by how firm the evidence is. It is no higher than a year ago. The second counts labs and large technology companies taking companies in the layers around them, by buying them or by hiring their teams: [fact:lab_deals_4q] such deals in the past four quarters. That tally is too young to set against the four quarters before it. Both tallies rise when coverage improves as well as when buying does, so neither is proof of anything on its own, and neither is used here to say that a named input has peaked.

The buying that is visible points at practice. In September 2025 TechCrunch reported that the leading labs were "demanding more" of what the industry calls reinforcement-learning environments: simulated software tasks in which a model's attempts are graded and the grades are used to train it. It said, citing The Information, that the leaders of Anthropic, another of the labs, had discussed spending more than a billion dollars on them within a year. A public directory that this site reads lists [fact:rl_vendor_count] firms selling them. A list of sellers is supply responding, though. It shows that the business exists, not that the product is short.

### Folio IV · the reading

## Most of the chain cannot be scored from what this site reads today

The scorecard below splits the making of AI into twenty-three inputs, from minerals to money, and asks of each how hard it is to get. The answer is a tightness score from nought to a hundred, read in five words from slack to severe. Each score is built from a few gauges. A gauge takes one published figure, such as how fast the supply of chip packaging is growing, and converts it to points on a scale set by hand. Beside each score is a confidence, worked out from how much of the intended evidence has a reading, how fresh it is and how good its source is. An input with no usable data is not given a middling score. It is withheld, with the reason. Today [fact:inputs_scored] of the twenty-three can be scored.

Most of the gauges behind the card read Epoch AI's estimates. One of its datasets follows the largest AI data centres, most of them in the United States, and gives for each a timeline of how much power the site draws or is expected to draw. At the [fact:dc_sites] sites where Epoch gives both a built figure and a planned one, the plans add up to [fact:dc_gap] what stands today. The card reads that as tight, with a caution attached: [fact:dc_sites_unbuilt] of those sites have nothing built at all yet, and without them the ratio is [fact:dc_gap_built]. Epoch publishes wide error margins for these estimates, so neither figure deserves its second decimal place. And a gap between plans and buildings is what a shortage of builders, equipment and grid connections would produce, but a fast and untroubled build-out would produce it too.

Where the record above and the card disagree, the card is usually measuring something slower. Its gauges for memory and AI chips read how fast the supply of memory is growing, how much of the chip supply one designer holds, and a long trend in the list prices of chips at launch. Epoch counts memory supply in dollars, so dearer memory looks the same as more memory. A shortage shows up first in what buyers pay today and how long they wait, and this site reads no series of either for these inputs. So the card can read an input as moderate while the record says it is short. The score for electricity measures demand only: how fast the power drawn by all the AI chips sold so far is growing, which says nothing about how much power can be supplied. Whenever it has a score, that score is drawn hatched, which on the scorecard marks low confidence. Money reads slack: the five largest builders of data centres have raised their spending on buildings and equipment by [fact:capex_growth] in a year.

[plate:scorecard]

### Folio V · the blind spots

## What nobody publishes is a list of where it may go next

Go back to the second condition. An input that has not yet become an industry has no quoted price and no public data. So the inputs this site cannot score because nobody publishes a series that would measure them are, as a group, candidates for the next bottleneck. They include the work done on a model after its first training, the expert-written data and practice tasks that work consumes, and the testing that says whether any of it helped. This is a conjecture, and it is stated as one. An absence of data is sometimes only an absence.

The same caution applies to the inputs that are scored. Memory supply grew by [fact:hbm_supply_growth] in a year, in dollars, which could mean far more memory or the same memory at a higher price. The grid is invisible from its supply side: this site reads what AI chips would draw, and nothing about what power stations and transmission lines can deliver. In both cases the fix is a better series, not a stronger opinion.

### Folio VI · the predictions

## What binds now, what binds next, and what would prove each wrong

Three cautions belong with any list like the one below. Rent from a bottleneck is temporary by construction, so every entry on it expires. The revenue figures quoted for the firms that sell training data are gross, not net: they count the pay that goes on to the people doing the work. And one risk sits under all of it. The largest builders are spending [fact:capex_to_revenue] as much on buildings and equipment as the AI revenue this site can measure. If that spending stopped, every input on this page would loosen at once, and the question of which was tightest would stop mattering for a while.

With that said, here is what this site expects, and what would show it to be wrong. Each entry is tested every night where a test exists. Where none does, the entry says what outcome would settle it.

exits.label: AI is not an ordinary technology
exits.text: AI stops looking like an ordinary technology if three things happen together. Models become nearly as reliable on long jobs as on short ones, and not just because the tests have run out of longer tasks. Most of the labour-market trackers we follow break at the same time. And either the share of work hours done with AI passes a fifth, or productivity runs well above trend for years on end.

exits.label: Profit moves up to the labs
exits.text: The chip makers' hold on the profit loosens if, over a year, the labs' share of the gross profit we can measure rises by five points while the chip makers' share falls by as much.

exits.label: Users keep most of the value
exits.text: Users rather than sellers keep most of the value if what people say they would need to be paid to give AI up is more than double the revenue the leading labs and business buyers bring in.

exits.label: AI speeds up its own invention
exits.text: AI starts speeding up its own invention if independent tests show agents doing more than a day of research work for each day a person puts in, and needing a person's help on long tasks less than half the time.

exits.label: Workers stop sharing the gains
exits.text: The case that workers share in AI's gains fails if the typical full-time worker's pay, after inflation, sits below its level at the end of 2022, just before ChatGPT, for four quarters running while the economy's output keeps growing. Pascual Restrepo, an economist who models work once machines can do every task, finds that workers' total pay never falls below its level before such AI unless something else, such as market power over computing, gets in the way; the typical worker's pay is the nearest measure this site reads.

capture.claim: So far, the profit is staying with the chip makers

diffusion.claim: Nothing yet shows AI spreading faster than an ordinary technology

predictions.claim: Data-centre buildings and their power hookups are the bottleneck.
predictions.text: Epoch expects more than twice the built power at the sites it tracks: [fact:dc_gap] today. Proved wrong if that ratio falls below two while at least twenty sites still compare. Only Epoch's revisions can take it below two, by raising what it counts as built or by cutting what it expects. The calendar moves it as well, because a milestone Epoch projected counts as built once its date passes, whether or not Epoch has confirmed it, and a site with no later milestone leaves the count. A fast, untroubled build-out would read the same as a shortage, so this is a weak test of a strong claim.

predictions.claim: Money is not what is scarce.
predictions.text: The five largest builders of data centres are still raising their spending by more than a fifth a year: [fact:capex_growth]. Proved wrong if that growth falls below a fifth, the halfway point on this site's scale for money: below it the reading leans towards scarce.

predictions.claim: Memory and chip packaging are short.
predictions.text: This cannot be tested yet. Memory supply is published in dollars, so a price rise and a volume rise look the same, and packaging supply is published without any measure of demand. It would be proved wrong if memory supply counted in units grew faster than chip shipments for two quarters running.

predictions.claim: Practice tasks with automatic graders, and the expert-written data they consume, are where the shortage goes next.
predictions.text: The test is whether the labs' disclosed buying from the firms that sell these inputs is rising on a year before. It is not, so this prediction is failing its test today. The tally is kept by hand from public announcements, and most such buying is never announced, so the test undercounts. It is still the only one available.

predictions.claim: Proof of what an AI agent (a model that carries out tasks with software tools on a person's behalf) did, and who answers for it, becomes a bottleneck once agents handle money.
predictions.text: This cannot be tested yet, because no public series exists. In April 2025 Mastercard and Visa each announced a system for verifying an AI agent before it pays on a person's behalf. The prediction would be proved wrong if the card networks' own systems come to cover this before any specialist firm sells it to a lab or a large company.

inputs.name: Critical minerals
inputs.what: Gallium, germanium, rare earths, copper and the other raw materials chips and power equipment are made from.

withheld.because: This site reads no series on how much of these minerals is mined or sold.

inputs.ceiling_rationale: Set low on purpose. The only gauge here measures demand for power, not its supply, so the score is a stand-in and is drawn hatched.

gauges.label: Growth in the power drawn by AI chips sold
gauges.scale_rationale: Growth of a quarter a year or less is the kind of new load a grid plans for in the ordinary way. A doubling within a year is more than new power stations can be built to serve in that time, which is when electricity stops being a bill and becomes a limit.

inputs.name: Electricity generation
inputs.reads: Demand only: how fast the electricity that all AI chips sold so far would draw is growing. It says nothing about how much power can be supplied.
inputs.what: The power stations, turbines, reactors and solar farms the electricity comes from.

inputs.name: The grid and its hookups
inputs.what: Transformers, switchgear, transmission lines and the queue to be connected. The wire between a power station and a rack of chips.

withheld.because: Grid operators publish their connection queues, but this site does not read them yet.

inputs.ceiling_rationale: Lower than the prototype's. Half of this ratio is Epoch's projection of sites not yet finished, and Epoch publishes wide error margins for its power figures.

gauges.label: Planned power against built power
gauges.scale_rationale: A ratio near one means about as much stands as Epoch expects at the sites it tracks. Two or three times is ordinary for a growing business whose projects take years. Past four, far more is planned than stands, which is what a shortage of builders, equipment and grid connections would produce, though a fast, untroubled build-out would read the same. It measures the gap between plans and buildings, not demand, and the age limit is four months because Epoch revises the file about monthly.

gauges.label: Growth in built power

unfed.because: Built power at the sites Epoch tracks grows very fast partly because Epoch chooses sites that are growing, so it says little about the market as a whole.

inputs.name: Data-centre buildings
inputs.reads: The power Epoch expects at the large sites it tracks, against the power it counts as built there today.
inputs.what: The shells, cooling and power hookups that racks of chips sit in.

inputs.name: Chip-making equipment
inputs.what: The machines that print, deposit, etch and inspect chips, made by a handful of firms such as ASML.

withheld.because: The equipment makers file their orders and backlogs, but this site does not read them yet.

inputs.ceiling_rationale: Kept from the prototype: a direct supply estimate from a careful source, though only an estimate.

gauges.label: Growth in leading-edge logic supply
gauges.scale_rationale: Runs backwards: faster supply growth means a looser input. New foundry capacity takes years to build, so growth of a fifth a year is already fast for this business, and flat supply while demand races is the tight end.

inputs.name: Chip foundries
inputs.reads: How fast the supply of leading-edge logic wafers is growing, year on year.
inputs.what: The factories, above all TSMC's, that make the most advanced logic chips.

inputs.ceiling_rationale: Kept from the prototype: two gauges from one careful source, both estimates.

gauges.label: Growth in packaging supply
gauges.scale_rationale: Runs backwards: faster supply growth means a looser input. Packaging lines can be added faster than foundries, so this scale asks for more: supply that doubles in a year is real relief, and supply that stands still while demand rises is the worst case.

gauges.label: How concentrated the buyers are
gauges.scale_rationale: When one buyer takes most of the supply, everyone else is rationed even if the total looks adequate. The index is the sum of the squared shares: a quarter means several buyers of similar size, and above a half one buyer sets the terms.

inputs.name: Advanced chip packaging
inputs.reads: How fast packaging supply is growing, and how much of it a few buyers take.
inputs.what: The step that joins processor dies to stacks of fast memory on one base. Nearly all of it is TSMC's process, called CoWoS.

inputs.ceiling_rationale: Kept from the prototype, which set it below the other chip inputs because the supply is counted in dollars, not units.

gauges.label: Growth in memory supply, in dollars
gauges.scale_rationale: Runs backwards: faster supply growth means a looser input. Because the supply is counted in dollars, which mixes volume with price, the scale is gentler than a true volume scale would be: even growth of four fifths a year reads only as easing.

gauges.label: Memory per unit of computing power

unfed.because: Epoch publishes each chip's memory, but this site does not read that column yet, and the prototype's scale for it was wrong by many orders of magnitude and would have to be rebuilt.

inputs.name: Memory
inputs.reads: How fast the supply of high-bandwidth memory is growing. Epoch counts it in dollars, so a price rise looks the same as more memory.
inputs.what: The fast stacked memory, called high-bandwidth memory, that sits beside an AI chip, made by SK Hynix, Samsung and Micron.

inputs.ceiling_rationale: Kept from the prototype: two gauges from one careful source, one an estimate of each designer's chip sales and one a long trend in the prices chips were released at. The gauge on chips for rent is left unfed.

gauges.label: How concentrated chip supply is by designer
gauges.scale_rationale: A single designer supplying most AI computing power leaves buyers no substitute, so that designer's choices about who gets chips become the market's supply. The index is the sum of the squared shares; well above four fifths is in effect one supplier.

gauges.label: Yearly change in the cost of computing power
gauges.scale_rationale: The cost of a unit of computing power has fallen steeply with each generation of chips. Steep falls mean the input is loosening in the way that matters to buyers; a fall that stalls or reverses is what a supply that cannot keep up produces. The reading is a trend over more than a decade, so it moves slowly, and its age limit is long because few new chips have a published price.

gauges.label: Chips available to rent

unfed.because: The one free feed of chips for rent returns a fixed page of offers, so counting them measures the page, not the market.

inputs.name: AI chips
inputs.reads: How much of the chip supply one designer holds, and whether the cost of a unit of computing power is still falling.
inputs.what: The processors that train and run models, from NVIDIA, AMD, Google, Amazon and others.

inputs.name: Networking and optics
inputs.what: The switches, cables and optical links that join thousands of chips into one machine.

withheld.because: This site reads no series on networking gear for AI clusters.

gauges.label: Activity in the open-source projects

unfed.because: The activity of the open-source projects is public, but this site does not read it, and more activity could mean either a shortage being fixed or none at all.

inputs.name: Systems software
inputs.what: The low-level programs, such as NVIDIA's CUDA, that let models run fast on a given chip.

withheld.because: The activity of the open-source projects is public, but this site does not read it, and more activity could mean either a shortage being fixed or none at all.

gauges.label: How fully training runs use their chips

unfed.because: Epoch publishes how fully some training runs used their chips, but this site does not read that column yet.

inputs.name: Training infrastructure
inputs.what: The software and know-how that keep tens of thousands of chips working on one training run without wasting them.

withheld.because: Epoch publishes how fully some training runs used their chips, but this site does not read that column yet.

gauges.label: Growth in the computing power behind the largest model

unfed.because: The largest training run on Epoch's list of frontier models is still its own estimate for xAI's Grok model of July 2025. Labs no longer disclose this figure and Epoch has not yet estimated newer models, so a record that stands still says nothing about whether growth has stopped.

inputs.name: Building frontier models
inputs.what: The labs that train the largest models, such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, xAI and Meta.

withheld.because: The largest training run on Epoch's list of frontier models is still its own estimate for xAI's Grok model of July 2025. Labs no longer disclose this figure and Epoch has not yet estimated newer models, so a record that stands still says nothing about whether growth has stopped.

inputs.name: Post-training
inputs.what: Everything done to a model after its first training to make it useful, including practice tasks with automatic graders and feedback from experts.

withheld.because: Nobody publishes what this work costs or how long buyers wait for it. This site counts the sellers and keeps a tally of disclosed deals, which says the business exists, not whether it is short.

inputs.name: Continual learning
inputs.what: Getting a model to keep learning from its use after release without forgetting what it knew.

withheld.because: No public test measures whether a model keeps learning after release. This site tracks what vendors claim, which is not a measure of scarcity.

inputs.ceiling_rationale: Kept from the prototype: list prices are observed, not estimated.

gauges.label: Cheapest model in the basket
gauges.scale_rationale: Read on a scale where each knot is four times the last, because this price has fallen by whole multiples, not by percentages. Below about a dollar for a million tokens of output (a token is a word or a piece of one), the cost of running a model stops deciding what gets built; at thirty times that, cost is the limit on what products are possible. The reading is the price list as last fetched, so its age runs from the last successful fetch.

gauges.label: Change in that price over a month

unfed.because: A month's change needs a month of price history, and this store's began in September of 2026.

gauges.label: Chips available to rent

unfed.because: The one free feed of chips for rent returns a fixed page of offers, so counting them measures the page, not the market.

inputs.name: Running models
inputs.reads: The price, in dollars for a million tokens of output, of the cheapest model among a named basket of flagship models on one marketplace. A token is a word or a piece of one. One vendor sets it.
inputs.what: Serving a trained model to users, which the industry calls inference.

gauges.label: How widely model prices are spread

unfed.because: The spread of list prices is set almost entirely by one very expensive model, so it says nothing dependable about how much a router can save.

inputs.name: Routing between models
inputs.what: Services that send each request to whichever model is cheapest or best for it.

withheld.because: The spread of list prices is set almost entirely by one very expensive model, so it says nothing dependable about how much a router can save.

inputs.name: Tests and evaluations
inputs.what: The benchmarks and testing firms that say what a model can do.

withheld.because: This site holds many benchmark scores, but none of them measures whether good testing is itself in short supply.

gauges.label: Share of models that can use tools

unfed.because: The marketplace lists which models can use tools, but this site stores only their prices.

inputs.name: Agents and tool use
inputs.what: Models that carry out tasks by using software tools, for minutes or hours at a time.

withheld.because: The marketplace lists which models can use tools, but this site stores only their prices.

inputs.name: Training data
inputs.what: Text written or checked by paid experts, generated data, and licensed archives.

withheld.because: Sellers' revenues, which this site tracks from press reports, show activity. Nobody publishes prices or waiting times, which are what scarcity would show up in.

inputs.name: Deployment platforms
inputs.what: Companies that host and run models for other businesses.

withheld.because: No public series separates these platforms' capacity from the cost of running models, which the row for running models reads.

inputs.name: Applications
inputs.what: The products people and companies use, from coding assistants to legal and medical tools.

withheld.because: Most of these companies are private, and too few publish their finances to say how hard money is for them to raise.

inputs.ceiling_rationale: Kept from the prototype: filed figures, the best evidence on the card, but one gauge.

gauges.label: Growth in the largest builders' spending
gauges.scale_rationale: Runs backwards, and reads how plentiful money is, not whether it is well spent. Flat or falling spending means the money has turned and financing is what holds the build-out back. Spending that grows by half or more in a year means money is plentiful. The reading is a total over four quarters, so it turns about two quarters after a single quarter would.

inputs.name: Capital
inputs.reads: How fast Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Oracle are raising their spending on buildings and equipment, over the past four quarters against the four before.
inputs.what: The money behind all of it, above all the spending of the five largest builders of data centres.

kinds.name: Supply
kinds.tight_means: Tight means the thing itself is hard to get: supply is growing slowly, a few buyers take most of it, or far more is promised than built.

kinds.name: Know-how
kinds.tight_means: Tight means few people or firms can do it well yet, so skill rather than material is what is short.

kinds.name: Money
kinds.tight_means: Tight means money is hard to raise. Slack means it is plentiful, which is not the same as well spent.

method.confidence_floor_rationale: A backstop. A score this weakly supported would mislead, so it is withheld. Under these weights the coverage rule usually withholds an input first.
method.epoch_quarterly_rationale: The limit on Epoch's quarterly chip gauges is set by the publisher's calendar. When Epoch last updated its chip-components file, the newest complete quarter in it was already more than two quarters old. This site has read only that one version, so it cannot yet say how often a newer quarter arrives. Its chip-sales file lists newer quarters, but only for some designers, and a share or a total across designers is read only from a quarter in which every designer reported. A tighter limit would drop every one of these gauges for no reason but that calendar; this one admits a complete quarter until it is about eleven months old and drops the gauge after that, until a newer complete quarter arrives. It was widened by a month before any Epoch gauge had passed the earlier limit, to allow for the gap between a quarter's end and Epoch's release, which the single version read so far suggests is long.
method.grade_quality_rationale: An editorial table, not a measurement: it turns the site's evidence grade for a gauge's weakest input into a factor between nought and one. An audited annual filing counts in full; a quarterly filing, which is a company's own unaudited statement, counts for nine tenths, and a gauge takes the grade of its weakest row, so a total over four quarters is graded as a quarterly filing. A respected group's estimate, which is what most of these gauges rest on, counts for three quarters.
method.half_life_rationale: Freshness halves each time a reading ages by three quarters of its gauge's age limit, so a reading at its limit still counts for about two fifths and one past it is dropped.
method.hatch_rationale: A bar is hatched when its confidence is low. With these weights that happens only where an input's ceiling is set low, which is done on purpose for scores that rest on a stand-in.
method.min_coverage_rationale: An input scores only when at least about a third of its intended evidence has a usable reading.

reasons.confidence: The evidence behind it is too weak to show a score.
reasons.coverage: Too little of its intended evidence has a usable reading today.
reasons.nothing: None of its gauges has a usable reading today: each is missing or older than its age limit.
reasons.required: The gauge this input depends on has no usable reading today.

method.weights_rationale: Because the three are multiplied, one weak factor drags the whole figure down. Coverage and source quality count most, and about equally, because a score resting on a small part of the intended evidence, or on a weak source, is the easiest to misread; freshness counts least. The prototype also weighed the width of each source's error range and the agreement between news reports; this store carries neither, so those are left out and the rest are rescaled.

spans.because: From the 2012 contest win to the years when Google bought a research team for its people; a researcher then put the world's experts at about fifty. That people were what held the field back is this site's reading, and the end year is a judgement: no single event marks it.

In January 2020 researchers at OpenAI found that a language model improves predictably as its size, its training text and the computing power spent on it are scaled up together, which gave every lab a reason to want more chips. The paper says nothing about chip supply; reading these years as short is a judgement.
NVIDIA's sales to data centres more than tripled in the year to January 2024, while the research firm Omdia estimated waits of most of a year for servers built on its chips.
In July 2023 TSMC said its advanced packaging capacity was very tight; in May 2024 SK Hynix said its fast memory was sold out for that year and almost sold out for the next.

In 2022 DeepMind found large models had been given too little text for their size, and Epoch estimated the stock of high-quality text would run out within a few years, an estimate it later moved to 2028. Neither says text was what held labs back.

A 2022 OpenAI paper trained a model on feedback from a few dozen hired contractors; by the middle of 2023 data firms were recruiting people with expertise in law, finance and programming, and in 2025 Meta took a large minority stake in one of them. The sources report the buying, not a shortage.

OpenRouter, a marketplace for routing between models, says it started in early 2023. By early 2025 Epoch found the price of a fixed level of performance falling many times over each year, so the price of using a model stopped being what held builders back.

In September 2025 TechCrunch reported the leading labs demanding more simulated tasks in which a model's attempts are graded, and said, citing The Information, that one lab's leaders had discussed spending more than a billion dollars on them within a year.

In July 2022 a Virginia utility began telling data-centre companies that power for some new sites would be delayed for years. In 2024 the United States Department of Energy reported that waits of three years were commonly quoted for large transformers; its report is not about data centres. That power is what holds the build-out back now is this site's prediction, listed below.

phase.rule: Installation while Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Oracle spend at least a dollar on buildings and equipment for each dollar of AI revenue we can measure, and deals in which a seller also funds its buyer are still being signed; deployment once that spending falls below half a dollar per dollar and fewer such deals are signed than a year before; a turning point in between. A change counts only after two quarters in a row agree, and the phase is untestable when either series has no reading.

slow_variables.sentence: The share of American businesses that used AI anywhere in the business in the past two weeks, from the Census Bureau's fortnightly business survey.

slow_variables.label: Work hours done with AI

slow_variables.label: Output per hour
slow_variables.sentence: How much more American businesses outside farming produce per hour worked than a year before. If AI is rearranging work, this is where it finally has to show up.

slow_variables.sentence: What Americans say they would need to be paid to give up AI chatbots, added up over a year. Value users keep is value no company gets to charge for.
